issues: 'coded by Aaron Swartz with Kevin Poulsen' suggests Poulsen co-wrote the code. The FPF release says the system was 'originally coded by the late transparency advocate Aaron Swartz' and 'created by Swartz in partnership with investigative reporter Kevin Poulsen'. SecureDrop's own FAQ says it was 'developed by Aaron Swartz' and that 'Kevin Poulsen originally managed the project'. The summary is reworded so that Swartz wrote it and Poulsen partnered on and managed it.

'kept its installation' is correct for October 2013 (FPF: 'will continue to operate its system'). However, the New Yorker article now carries 'Update: The New Yorker is no longer using Strongbox.' The summary is reworded so readers do not take this as still true.

Checked and correct: date 15 October 2013 and San Francisco dateline, rename to SecureDrop, codename mechanism, University of Washington audit (led by Alexei Czeskis), New Yorker Strongbox launch on 14 May 2013 (page datePublished 2013-05-14), and 'four months after the first Snowden stories' (June 2013).

fieldFixes.summary: Four months after the first Snowden stories, the Freedom of the Press Foundation announced on 15 October 2013 that it had taken over DeadDrop, the whistleblower-submission system coded by Aaron Swartz in partnership with the journalist Kevin Poulsen, who managed the project, renamed it SecureDrop and would install it in newsrooms. Each source receives a codename so they can keep talking to a newsroom without revealing their identity or using e-mail. The code had been audited by University of Washington researchers; The New Yorker, the first user since May 2013 under the name Strongbox, was to keep running its installation.

issues: The summary says the Times 'revealed that the start-up Clearview AI had scraped more than three billion images from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo, Twitter and other sites'. The original article, read via Gulf News's syndicated copy of the NYT text dated 19 January 2020, hedges this: 'a database of more than 3 billion images that Clearview claims to have scraped from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo and millions of other websites'. Twitter does not appear anywhere in that text. It comes from EPIC's paraphrase, which cites the Times article's 10 February 2020 update.

The '600 agencies' figure was the company's own claim and was not independently verified: 'more than 600 law enforcement agencies have started using Clearview in the past year, according to the company, which declined to provide a list.'

'New Jersey's attorney general barred state police from using it' is too narrow and ambiguous, since it can be read as the New Jersey State Police only. The ACLU says the AG 'prohibited state law enforcement from using Clearview’s system'. EPIC says New Jersey 'banned statewide law enforcement agencies', and the NYT follow-up is headlined 'New Jersey Bars Police From Using Clearview Facial Recognition App'.

Checked and correct: Vermont AG lawsuit and congressional demands (ACLU), OAIC preliminary inquiries on 21 January 2020, and the October 2021 cease-collection and destroy orders. The OAIC determination is cited as [2021] AICmr 54 (14 October 2021), but the PDF's signature block reads '22 October 2021'. Either way 'October 2021' holds.

fieldFixes.summary: The New York Times article 'The Secretive Company That Might End Privacy as We Know It' by Kashmir Hill, dated 18 January 2020 in its web address, revealed that the start-up Clearview AI had built a face-search app on a database of more than three billion images it claimed to have scraped from Facebook, YouTube, Venmo and millions of other websites, and that — according to the company — more than 600 law-enforcement agencies had started using it in the past year. After the story, New Jersey's attorney general barred the state's police from using it, Vermont's attorney general sued and members of Congress demanded answers; Australia's privacy regulator opened inquiries on 21 January 2020 and in October 2021 ordered the company to stop collecting and to destroy Australians' images.

issues: Summary calls the 1994 cryptography item 'a panel on cryptography and privacy'. The 2600 store listing shows it was a session titled 'Cryptography and Privacy' introduced by Bob Stratton, with a Clipper Chip (AT&T 3600 Surety) demonstration by Bernie S. and John Turbo and also featuring Eric Hughes and Matt Blaze. 2600 titles its real panels explicitly ('The 2600 Panel', 'The Author Panel', 'The Cellular Panel'), and this one is not billed as a panel. The wording is changed to 'session'. The Clipper demonstration is left out of the summary because the listing is a programme description written in the future tense ('will attempt').
'Modelled on the Dutch hacker gatherings' overstates the source, which says only 'inspired by'.

'the first US hacker conference on that scale' is HOPE's own claim ('the first time that a hacker conference of this size had been attempted in the United States'). The summary now attributes it to the organisers.

Dates (13-14 August 1994), venue (Hotel Pennsylvania), attendance (well over 1,000), 2600's tenth anniversary and 'annual from 2025' are all confirmed on the cited pages. Wikipedia independently gives 'August 13-14, 1994', 'Over 1,000 people attended'.

fieldFixes.summary: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly marked its tenth anniversary with Hackers On Planet Earth, held at the Hotel Pennsylvania in Manhattan on 13–14 August 1994 and attended by well over 1,000 people. Inspired by the Dutch hacker gatherings of the 1980s and 1990s, it was, by its organisers' account, the first hacker conference of that size attempted in the United States, with talks 'ranging from privacy issues to technology to politics' and a 'Cryptography and Privacy' session featuring Eric Hughes and Matt Blaze. HOPE became a recurring New York conference, annual from 2025.
